en: Commentary: Regarding "the perception of a young girl" and so forth: in the Western Regions, it is established as a ritual that encountering a young girl signifies auspiciousness.
Furthermore, it is said that a young girl has white teeth, thin lips, and slender yet well-rounded ankles and knees.
This indicates that the woman will surely give birth to a virtuous child. If the signs differ from those mentioned above, she will surely give birth to an evil child.
Commentary.
However, regarding the "definitive contradiction" (*niyata-virodha*) with arising and so forth:

it is called "definitive contradiction" because it contradicts those [factors] by way of being definitively distinct from them, since it negates that arising and so forth definitely exist as something separate.

This is not the same as the sixth type of "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñā-virodha*), which consists of contradicting the opponent's own position by means of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the reason (*hetu*), or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Some say that even without modifying the reason, the sixth [type] can still be established. To this we reply in detail:
This is not so. Otherwise, what further distinction would there be between the first and sixth types of indeterminate [factors]?
Therefore, the initial explanation is correct.
Commentary:
Regarding the passage from "The unconditioned is non-arising" up to "the three kinds of defining characteristics," this is an objection raised by an outsider.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "the essence has no arising or ceasing," this is the Master of the Treatise’s response.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "this objection is not so," etc., it asks:
"The words of the opponent are likewise."

Question: If there is a distinction between establishing [a conventional designation] and not establishing it, how can you resolve this objection? Answer: In our school, even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, fascicle twenty, states:
The unconditioned dharma has three characteristics:
namely, non-arising, non-ceasing, and non-abiding.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 88, states:
The conditioned is impermanent;
the three characteristics of the conditioned are established and can be apprehended.

One should know that the opposite of this—the unconditioned—is permanent and possesses three characteristics. If so, why are there only twenty-four factors dissociated from mind? The answer is: they are stated as twenty-four by mentioning only the most prominent ones.
Since I have provisionally granted this [premise],
you should establish it in reality;
furthermore, I shall challenge those six [positions].
In our school, because the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is one and without differentiation, it possesses no provisional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*).
In your school, you admit that cessation (*nirodha*) and so forth have multiple essences; like the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they possess many real characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Commentary:

Regarding "there being near and distant causes," this means that among the six causes, with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five are all subsumed under the condition of cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, homogeneous causes consist of the three natures and the five aggregates, each acting as a cause for itself.
For example, a wholesome aggregate of consciousness is proximate with respect to itself,
whereas it is termed remote with respect to the other four aggregates.
Because it is not consciousness; the relative intimacy or distance between the remaining [factors] when viewed in relation to one another should be understood accordingly.
Commentary.
The same applies to the conditions for phenomena (*dharmas*).
Among the four conditions, all except the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) are termed "conditions.

Furthermore, when the six sense organs (*indriyas*) are considered in relation to their respective six consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), they are called the immediate and predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The remaining [bases] are termed "distant" in relation to the six consciousnesses because they do not act as obstacles and are not proximate causes for their arising.
The rest should be understood accordingly.
[In the] Commentary:
"When the masters of the *Nyāya* reach this point, they adopt [this view]."
According to the meaning of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 14:
the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) in the future merely initiates its capacity (*śakti*), but it is not yet an activity (*kāritra*).
It is only when it presently exerts the function of grasping an effect (*phala-grahaṇa*) that it constitutes an activity.
"Activity must have capacity, but capacity does not necessarily have activity"— this is the refutation by the Abhidharmakośa masters.
"Capacity" and "activity" are merely different names for the same thing.
Why is it that arising is designated merely as a "capacity" (śakti),
while the three [characteristics] beginning with duration are called "functions" (kāritra)?
Furthermore, this contradicts the explanation provided by the Sautrāntika masters.
It is said that there is no equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) that takes its fruit at one time and gives its fruit at another time.
According to that master of the treatise,
entering the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) constitutes precisely the taking and giving of fruit in the past.
If that which has already passed were to take [an object], it should be called "present. The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) states:
"To say that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) takes the past all at once while giving it gradually is untenable."
This implies that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) apprehends [its object] at a different time, which contradicts the earlier *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
[The commentary asks:
Why [is it said that] past and future dharmas all possess functional capacity?

This objection is difficult to overcome: it is not the case that all phenomena possess functional capacity solely for the purpose of producing their own characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their effects; rather, they possess them because these capacities are co-existent with the phenomena from the very beginning.
"Arising from conditions,
not from activity, etc."—
this restates the opponent's position in order to establish the meaning of the preceding refutation.
Based on your original statement that "arising and the fruit are equal," this refers to functional capacity (*śakti*) rather than manifest activity (*kāritra*),
because you did not state that other dharmas possess such capacity.
Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) lacks active function.
Because it performs no activity, it is called "functional capacity" (*śakti*);
likewise, other future [dharmas] also lack activity,
and because they lack activity, they are called "functional capacity."
The dharma that is difficult to pass away should also be understood according to this principle.
[In the] Commentary:
"When 'dissimilar cessation' (visabhāga-nirodha) arrives, it is no longer present."
Question: According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the three [characteristics] of duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*bhaṅga*) are all capable of grasping a fruit;
their functions for arising are each distinct.
Regarding the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya-dharma*), "abiding" causes them to remain stable and attain superior results;
"alteration" causes them to decline and attain inferior results;
and "cessation" causes them to perish and enter the past.
Is this objection not a fault? Answer: Because [factors] such as "difference" (visabhāga) cannot induce a superior fruit, they are said not to "take the fruit.
Even if one objects from this particular perspective, there is no error.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states that the three dharmas of the future possess functional activity (*kāritra*).
According to that treatise, it says:
"Regarding all phenomena that possess functional activity in the future,
there are generally three categories."
The first is internal phenomena,
such as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). The second is external phenomena.
Like the light of the moon.

Regarding the three internal and external phenomena, they are like all conditioned characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Question: What is the function of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)? Answer: That same treatise states:

The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) can correctly abandon the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). That is to say, at the moment it is about to arise, it abandons the state of being an ordinary person;
and in the stage of its actual cessation, it is able to sever the ten types of proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm. [Commentary:]
That which is called "arising" refers to the future life;
the relinquishing of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) in the future life is the function of patience (*kṣānti*).
The other two [cases] may be understood accordingly. Regarding the commentary’s statement,
"that is, the previous [cases of] 'the dissimilar [reason] is unestablished' and so forth":
According to that treatise,
the Sautrāntika school refutes the Sarvāstivāda as follows:
"It is logically untenable for something distinct from a single dharma to exist, whether one analyzes it through its progression or its regression."
"Difference" refers to the transformation of nature and characteristics over time;
it cannot be said that this very phenomenon is different from itself.
Therefore, a verse says:
Thus, the prior [state] and the subsequent [state] cannot be established as different;
being different from the prior, they are not a single dharma.
Therefore, with respect to a single dharma, [the two are not distinct].
"Establishing difference ultimately does not succeed. Commentary:

Regarding the characteristic of difference and the phenomenon that is different, if these are identical to the previously mentioned characteristic of duration and the phenomenon that endures, then the meaning of "difference" is not established.
Because it is not a separate dharma.
This is a further challenge:
if the dharma characterized by difference were distinct from the dharma that abides in the prior characteristic of abiding.
Dharmas are not unitary.
If they were distinct while abiding in different dharmas,
there would be the fault of contradicting one's own tenet.
This is a reductio ad absurdum, because he [the opponent] admits that a single dharma possesses both abiding and change.
(Commentary)
Regarding the ten temporal stages:
there are five stages each within the womb and outside the womb,
both of which correspond to the numerical categories of the Dharma.
Commentary:
The various treatises refer exclusively to the former [case],
whereas the various treatises universally clarify all sentient beings.
The term "sentient beings" also includes those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Since the final mind of one beyond training has no further aggregates, there is nothing subsequent that could differ from it; therefore, it is said to be "in relation to what precedes."
The Commentary (*Śāstra*) also states, "excluding that final mind":
this refers to excluding that very last mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Since one also attains a different state from other sentient beings,
there is no contradiction. Thus says the treatise.
If names, phrases, and phonemes are not truly expressive, one might ask:

"Does the Mahāyāna itself not commit the fallacy of its own inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)? For it is admitted that even matter (*rūpa*) in the Buddha-fields of other directions is expressive, existing as something distinct from sound.
Answer: There is no inconclusiveness, because the term "truly expressive" was used specifically to exclude those [non-linguistic cases]. Therefore, the fallacy does not apply.
Commentary:
If one did not mention the "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana) and so forth,
and if the thesis merely stated that there is no separate substantial entity apart from its basis;
He asserts that curvature exists as a distinct substantial entity separate from its supporting matter;
therefore, his position lacks the probandum. If he says it is [contained within] the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), [the same fault applies].
He also does not permit that curvature upon form (rūpa) should exist within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Therefore, the analogy is without fault.
[Commentary].
Regarding the objection that "the essence of the precepts (śīla-tattva) depends solely upon volition (cetanā) and so forth," the intent of the external critic is as follows:
[If that were so,] longevity and so forth would depend solely upon form (rūpa).
One should immediately order it to be collected in a separate place;
since the non-manifest (avijñapti) depends solely on volition (cetanā),
it should not be gathered in the same location.
The meaning of the answer is as follows:
Since non-manifestation (avijñapti) shares the same locus as volition (cetanā) within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
how can you raise the objection that they must not share the same locus?
This is merely answering him based on their being in the same location, so as not to avoid his challenge.
He challenges it, saying:
"The same applies to long and short."
Because they are manifested in the same location, how can one raise the objection that they should be in separate locations?
From this point forward, the correct explanation shall follow. Some say:
The manifest activity is the objective sphere (ālambana).
Since that which depends upon it is also the objective sphere, they are both subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana). Detailed explanation:
The principle that the non-informative [matter] of meditative concentration and the path may be so is acceptable;
however, how can the non-informative [matter] of the Prātimokṣa depend on the present?
Furthermore, if the object of the mind were identical to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), [there would be no separate sphere for the sense objects].
Since forms and so forth, being curved or bent, are themselves objects of the mental consciousness,
they ought to belong solely to the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana); therefore, it is known that [your position] is incorrect.
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "This should be like those [cases of] sound and so forth," the sub-commentary (*shu*) presents two interpretations.
The initial establishment of the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) refutes [the opponent's position]; as for the phrase "this," it refers to this small internal sound,
and "that" likewise refers to that small sound of stringed instruments.
Next, regarding the phrase "furthermore, if [it is] speech-sound and so forth," this refers to the internal, inwardly turning sound;
that, in turn, is the name-sound produced internally and externally.
However, in the commentary (*śāstra*), the "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is distinguished from the preceding external measure as the subject (*dharmin*);
this can be understood through reflection.
[End of] Commentary.
Regarding the statement that "the two types of karma, such as the speech of a transformation body," the intention is explained by way of the analogy of a lamp.

Question: If it is granted that that which expresses constitutes vocal karma (*vākkarman*), Answer: In the Mahāyāna, the substantial entity (*dravya*) of vocal karma is exclusively volition (*cetanā*).
If one relies on the perspective of conventional karma, there is no fault in designating even sounds that are detached from their physical substance as "karma.
Therefore, the seventh fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The vocal karma of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) each has three types."
That is to say, they correspond to one's own body and another's body, as well as that which is not the body.
Mental karma consists of only two types: namely, those pertaining to one's own body and those pertaining to another's body.
There is nothing that is not the body; "non-body" refers to that which is insentient (*acetana*).
Since that which is associated with the mind is not insentient, there are only these two types.
Question: Can the transformative speech (*nirmāṇavāk*) of the Hīnayāna constitute karma? Answer: According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it can.
That is to say, vocal expression (*vāg-vijñapti*) is capable of producing names and so forth;
this is the nature of vocal karma (*vāk-karman*). If one were to exclude vocal expression, [the production of names and so forth would not occur].
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two interpretations. One states that the nature of emanated speech is vocal karma;
because it is produced by the mind, although it arises as an emanation detached from a physical basis, it is nonetheless without appropriation (*anupātta*).
However, as these belong to sentient beings and are not comprised within the external vessel-world,
the sounds of the external vessel-world— such as those of the wind-mandala and so forth—
are contrary to this and cannot function as signifiers.
The same applies to sounds such as those from stringed instruments and pipes; they likewise lack denotative power.
While songs and the like resemble names, they are not actual [names];
we admit them to be vocal sounds.
Because it is produced by wind, breath, and so forth,
although it is called "speech-sound," it is nonetheless subsumed under the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
There is nothing that is not a form which is not karma.
Because it is not established [as a real entity], the second [position] states: although these are indeed designators, they lack real names;
all that expresses is like a name but not real, just as fire in a mirror resembles fire but is not actual fire.
The nature [of these] is also not karma,
nor is it fully accomplished,
because they arise from great elements that are non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
The various treatises rely on the semblance [of reality] to speak of "sentient beings" (*sattva*);
based on the transformation of the substance itself, they speak of "transformed speech.
(Commentary)
Regarding the phrase "now, in the Mahāyāna, the causes are equal," according to the *Abhidharmapitaka* (First Section), it says:
"The cause that receives the great elements (*mahābhūta*)."
That is to say, sounds such as speech;
those caused by non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are,
for example, sounds such as those from trees.
"Caused by both" refers to sounds such as those of hands and drums. The commentary states:
"Cause" means the reason.
"Appropriated" (upātta) means grasped; it is called "appropriated" because it is perceived.
That is to say, sound produced by the internal primary elements is included within the category of sentient beings.
The opposite of not receiving sound can be understood by reversing the preceding [explanation].
Sound induced by internal and external conditions is called "concurrent" (*sāmagrī*).
A single sound is produced by two predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
However, there is a school that does not accept this;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states:
"There is no such thing as the nature of a single sound, because it has as its causes both appropriated and non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
Because the two sets of four great elements each produce their own distinct effects,
although these two sets of great elements may strike against one another, they act as causes to produce sounds separately;
thus, with respect to their respective bases, they do not constitute three entities.
Although two sounds arise from the cause of hands striking cymbals against one another,
they mutually obscure each other such that one may perceive only a single type; thus,
their distinction is difficult to discern.
Therefore, the sphere of sound consists of only two types.
Now, following the Mahāyāna,
we do not adopt the Lesser Vehicle's interpretation.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "just as with the sound of a forest, the preaching of the Dharma can also be categorized as wholesome and so forth," that which occurs within the Buddha’s transformative influence is subsumed under the category of the wholesome.
The remainder is not so,
because the Buddha’s physical form and voice are exclusively wholesome. According to one interpretation, even if it were not a transformation,
there would be such sounds in the external vessel-world produced by the superior karma of sentient beings.
The ability to express all phenomena is like the sound of strings and pipes;
there is likewise no error here. In detail:
the sutra states only that these were manifested by the Buddha.
The sounds of stringed and wind instruments require someone to blow or strike them;
since there is no precedent for such instruction, it is difficult to rely upon.
(Commentary)
Regarding the statement that "speech and names are neither identical nor distinct," this is intended to refute the following objection: "If you do not admit that my name is distinct from speech,
then since you do not admit they are distinct, you must admit they are identical."
Therefore, this answer was given. Regarding the phrase in the commentary,
"that which is beloved by the gods," etc.:
There are briefly two explanations: first, the celestial being (*deva*) belongs to that which loves, and love (*kāma*) belongs to that which is loved;
since it is the love of the celestial beings that is termed "heaven" (*svarga*).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Both "the two gods" and "love" belong to the category of the lover;
that which is now loved receives the name "loved by the gods," which is thus a *matup-purisa* (possessive determinative compound).
This matter is elucidated according to the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises;
it is precisely what is explained in the *Śūyao*.
[Commentary:]
Regarding the phrase "letters manifest meaning" and so forth:
names and phrases are the two types [of linguistic units] that manifest and reveal;
they do so by manifesting and revealing the meanings of both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific distinction (*viśeṣa*).
Since the phonemes (*vyañjana*) serve as the basis for the names (*nāman*), they are called "manifestation" (*vyañjanā*) by way of what depends upon them.
Some say that the essence of the phonemes is itself the manifestation, because they are able to express those two—names and phrases (*pada*).
"That which can express" (nengquan) means to manifest or reveal the meaning. The detailed commentary states:
"The explanation in the *Shu* (Commentary) is correct, for it has a basis."
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52, states:
"If one relies solely on the literal text, one may understand the phonetic syllables alone,
yet one will not be able to comprehend all the underlying facts and meanings."
If one relies upon names, one can indeed comprehend the intrinsic nature and specific characteristics of various phenomena,
as well as their phonetic qualities;
however, one cannot comprehend their profound and vast distinctions.
If one relies on the foundational syllables (*pada*), it should be known that all [phenomena] can be fully understood.
The fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Syllables such as *ka*, *a*, and so forth, are not expressive [of meaning]."
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 76, states:
"Phonemes (*vyañjana*) are that which cannot directly perceive the meaning;
they merely serve as the basis for names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*) to express the meaning."
In these various treatises, it is said that words and phrases cannot fully comprehend the meaning of things; they can only express phenomena (*dharma*).
How, then, can they be called "manifesting"? If names are what manifest, [how do they do so]?
Why is it said that one cannot understand the meaning of the events?

Therefore, the Commentary explains "skillful" (*śubha*). If so, why does [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] state in the fifty-second [fascicle]: "Regarding all objects of knowledge and all things expressed"?
The most abbreviated ideation is a phoneme (*vyañjana*);
if intermediate, it is a name (*nāman*);
if extensive, it is a phrase (*pada*). Answer: Because they serve as the basis and support for those names and phrases, enabling them to function as expressive communication.
There is a meaning to be expressed through distant [terms]. When the expression of that meaning is remote and subtle, it is termed "abbreviated" (*laghu*).
It is not that what is directly expressed is minor that it is called abbreviated. Now, another explanation is given:
If one says that the expressive [factors] consist only of names (nāman) and phrases (pada),
or if one says they extend to include phonemes (vyañjana) as well—
since phonemes can manifest the distinctions of tone and rhythm that constitute both names and phrases.
Therefore, the fifty-second [fascicle] states:
"If one relies solely on the literal text,
one can only comprehend the phonetic tones."
The *Xiǎnyáng shèngjiào lǜlùn* (12) states:
"Because it manifests names and phrases, it is called 'syllables' (*vyañjana*).
The *Abhidharmapitaka-prakaraṇa-śāstra* (2) states:"
The term "text" (*vyañjana*) is used here because it can manifest those two [meaning and name].
Furthermore, this term "name" (*nāman*) is employed because it manifests the meaning (*artha*). As for "meaning," it refers to the underlying reason or purpose.
The *vyañjana* (syllable) is that by which sound is manifested; it is the basis for the phonetic modulations of speech.
[In the] Commentary: "As for the statement that the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) do not have a pervasive essence (*svabhāva*):"
These two aspects do not mutually pervade one another; this is called "non-pervasion. [The Commentary states:
"That which is the essence of both self-nature and its specific distinctions is what is universally pervasive."
These two both pervade the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*);
therefore, they are called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*).
[Commentary].
Regarding the statement that "it is not the same as those [other systems]":
this treatise asserts that names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This differs from other teachings, which hold that the intrinsic nature of the self-essence of phenomena is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The commentary states: "From 'all phenomena' up to 'verified by direct perception alone,' it cites the very essence of the nature that is verified.
(Commentary)
If it is the case that all phenomena are ineffable and so forth, one might ask:
what is the distinction between this question and the subsequent question and answer? The answer is: the former is coarse and the latter is subtle;
thus, there is a distinction between the two.
One may realize this through careful reflection.
Commentary:
Furthermore, it is only the five sense organs, the five sense objects, the mind, and mental factors that can obtain [it].

The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), as well as their names (*nāman*), cannot be apprehended; therefore, only the mind (*citta*) apprehends them.
In the state of Buddhahood, all eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) apprehend them.
Among the eight [consciousnesses] within the causal stage, two obtain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*):

the five consciousnesses obtain only the specific characteristics of the five objects; the sixth and the five [sensory consciousnesses], when sharing the same object, obtain the specific characteristics of the objects.
The mental consciousness within meditative concentration also attains the five faculties;

others do not. Question: When the five faculties illuminate their objects, why do the five objects not themselves attain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Answer: A mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is said to attain its own specific characteristic.

Since the sense faculties (*indriya*) are not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they cannot apprehend that [object]. If this is so, why does the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state: "Question: To whom does such direct perception belong? Answer:
It belongs to those with direct perception of the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*)," and so forth?
According to that response, the essence of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) is also termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Why, then, do you now say it is not? Answer: The meaning of that passage cites the mind’s faculties and their objects.
One speaks of "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) because one considers that there can be a mind possessing direct perception.
However, the essence of direct perception is in reality nothing other than mental phenomena (caitta).
[Commentary]

That which cannot be distinguished from the common [characteristic] is the meaning of the differentiation of the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣārtha*), because it is obtained through the phrase-meaning of differentiation (*viśeṣārtha-pada*).
Question: Are these two—the name (*nāman*) and the phrase (*pada*)—the expressed meanings of the particular (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) and the common (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)?
What is the difference between the objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)? Answer: There are both similarities and differences.
First, regarding the mind of inference, there is a similarity in that it can generally take both of those [objects] as its objective support.
If it were not so, how could one say that "hearing" refers to inference? For inference,
based on this [direct perception], is able to take those two as its object.
As for what distinguishes it:
in order to understand specifically the particular and universal characteristics,
one employs mental marks and modes of engagement as actual analogies for other phenomena.
Only then is it called the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) apprehended by inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the point that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is similar to that [inference],
it merely means that names and phrases denote such things as form, sound, permanence, and impermanence.

Regarding the statement that these [objects] are perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa) through both their specific and general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa/sāmānyalakṣaṇa), yet are said to be distinct:
the referents of names and phrases are merely transformations of the mind and lack substantial reality;
they function solely as general characteristics.
Direct perception (pratyakṣa) carries with it a conceptual designation; those two characteristics are collectively termed the "particular characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, the mind of direct perception seeks out the phenomenon that is designated by that name and expression.
Although one does not definitively determine that names belong to meanings and so forth,
the manner in which one forms conceptual constructions is likewise the same;
for where sound does not reach, cognition does not arise.
The Buddha knows that because it lacks universal objectification (*sarvālambana*),
it is also the same as those [other states],
with the exception of the aforementioned meanings.
If the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness exist in their causal state,
they possess substantial reality according to the correct principle; however, the characteristics associated with meditative concentration may or may not possess substantial reality.
Because the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) denoted by names and phrases do not exist, they are distinct from those [particulars].
Question: The transformations of mind denoted by names and phrases lack intrinsic substance and function solely as common characteristics.
Inference is also like this.

What is the ultimate distinction between the two types of transformative consciousness and their two types of objects? Answer: The referents of terms and so forth that encompass all phenomena within their own respective classes are called "universal characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
The object of inference (anumāna) that extends across different categories is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
For example, the probans of being produced (kṛtakatva) applies to both sound and a pot.
Thus, the mind of inference establishes a single category that permeates other phenomena through comparison.
The mind that investigates words and so forth is not like this;

therefore, there is a distinction. If that is so, within which category of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the wisdom that investigates words and so forth subsumed? Answer: When the concentrated mind takes names as its object, it is subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Seeking names through arbitrary conceptualization is precisely the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*);

it is subsumed under what is not valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). If one does not engage in arbitrary conceptualization, then even if one does not apply mental attention (*amanasikāra*), [it is not pervasive imagination].
That which penetrates other phenomena is likewise subsumed under inference (*anumāna*).
Otherwise, under what category would this mind be included?

Consider further. Question: What is the difference between that which is expressed by names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), and the two characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) described in the Sūtras? Answer: The Sūtras rely upon the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena.

Names and phrases are established in the mind as conceptualizations (saṃjñā) that are expressed by them. Question: Why is it that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of the cognition which takes names and so forth as its objects is not taken as the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), but rather only the mental transformation consisting of the interpretative understanding (pratipatti) is taken? Answer: The objective aspect that is transformed does not extend to other categories [of beings]; therefore, it cannot be called "common."
Because its mode of activity and understanding extend to other [objects], it is called a "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Question:

Since this investigation (*vitarka*) is designated as "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and it relies upon a common characteristic whose essential nature is non-existent, how can there be the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*) capable of producing its own substantial body? Answer: The aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the wisdom that investigates names and phrases is not non-existent.
The mind that understands through conformative practice can give rise to the fundamental substance;
however, it merely forms understandings of blue, yellow, and so forth, or form, sound, and so forth, upon the level of appearances.
The common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) that serves as the objective referent for this understanding-mind is non-existent.
Because this is superimposed upon their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
there is further question and answer,
as fully explained in the chapter.
Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "not yet having understood that names exist," there are briefly two explanations. The first says: because one has not yet understood the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, one cannot obtain the existence of names.
The phrasing is concise.

The remainder should be explained accordingly. Second, although there are many syllables, they are still unable to bring about the understanding of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena; therefore, names (*nāman*) are required.
There is a phrase that follows this principle.
This clarifies the establishment of those three— names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)—
and does not take into account the reason for [the inclusion of] verses (*gāthā*).
Therefore, the concluding remark below states that no separate verses are recited;
this indicates that the latter interpretation is superior. Question: Names and phrases depend upon syllables, yet all three are mutually incompatible.
It is established only by depending on verses;
as for the inclusion of those that do not correspond to verses, there are two explanations.
The first is as analyzed in the commentary.
Second, syllables (vyañjana) constitute names (nāman), phrases (pada), and so forth;
they are said to be non-associated (viprayukta) because their force continues in succession.
Although a verse (gāthā) is constituted by phrases, [it is distinct from them].
Regarding the statement, "The intervals between [the moments] are not included therein," the commentary says:
"Although the two [aspects] are mutually inseparable from their own respective natures," and so forth.
These are the essential natures of the two types of unimpeded knowledge:
that of phenomena (*dharma*) and that of expression (*nirukti*). Their essence is exclusively wisdom (*prajñā*), though their respective objects differ.
The substance is not different.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the words correspond to the capacity [of the audience]," etc.:
Furthermore, for example, the Tathāgata is able to produce all sounds from a single voice to respond to the capacities of sentient beings. Regarding the commentary’s phrase,
"Having heard with the ear," and so forth:
This is divided into two parts based on the mode of practicing the hearing of the Dharma.
It is not that sound, names, and so forth possess two distinct substantial entities; rather, it may be understood as a statement that there is no difference in their essential nature.

This explains the two unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*). Regarding the commentary’s statement, "In all other Buddha-fields... up to establishing the three": * **Unhindered Analytical Knowledge of Phenomena** (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): This refers to the unimpeded knowledge of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and so forth, of all phenomena. * **Unhindered Analytical Knowledge of Expression** (*niruktipratisaṃvid*): This refers to the unimpeded knowledge of all languages, dialects, and modes of expression used by sentient beings. The phrase "up to establishing the three" indicates that these two analytical knowledges encompass the remaining three types of unhindered analytical knowledge—namely, those concerning eloquence (*pratibhāna*), meaning (*artha*), and phenomena (*dharma*)—thereby establishing the complete set of four. Thus, it is said that within all other Buddha-fields, these four unhindered analytical knowledges are fully established.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other sutras serve as proof for this. Question:
According to those sutras, it is said that the Tathāgata in my land has no verbal teaching;
rather, he causes all devas and humans to enter into the practice of the Dharma solely through various fragrances.

Question: Since names and so forth do not exist upon the fragrance itself, how can this serve as proof? Answer: It is said that those [names] do not exist in that land because they are established here in this land through the distortions of vocal sounds.

It is not said that those names, phrases, and so forth do not exist upon the fragrance. Question: What is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the names and so forth upon the fragrance? Answer: Because one realizes the distinctions in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena through the distinctions in the fragrance.

It is like sound being bent to explain the Dharma and so forth. Question: How are names and so forth established based on volition (*cetanā*) and the rest? Answer: Names and so forth are provisionally established based on volition and the rest, which apprehend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Question: If that is so, does the Buddha in that land preach the Dharma? Answer: He also preaches the Dharma. Question: How is it expressed such that others attain understanding, and why is it called "preaching"? Answer: It is because the speaker’s volition possesses names and so forth.
To cause those who are suitable vessels for transformation to give rise to the cognition of names through reflection upon the number of syllables and so forth is called "teaching.

Now, since the purpose of teaching the Dharma is fundamentally to cause others to understand, what fault is there in calling it "teaching" when it causes understanding to arise in others by means of conditions such as reflection? Question: Do those sentient beings then collectively obtain the minds of others?
Furthermore, how can those below know the intentions of those above? Answer: Since the worlds differ, what loss is there in this general principle?
It is not contradictory for those above to act upon those below and for those below to understand them accordingly. Question: In this world as well, one perceives forms.
Upon smelling the fragrance, one spontaneously contemplates and understands its meaning.
It should be established that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) depend upon such contemplation and so forth. Answer: There are two interpretations.
The first is based on the majority of cases.

The second [position] says: Because one has previously heard sounds and first understood the names (*nāman*) and so forth, when one later sees forms (*rūpa*) and the like, an understanding of the object arises;

this is because one recollects the names, phrases (*pada*), and so forth from that previous time. Question: Does this [explanation] apply to the understanding of odors (*gandha*) and the other [objects]?
Question: It is said that recollection depends on sound, while the understanding of others arises from the scent of the texts.
Yet, one likewise recalls the scent without it being a teaching. Answer: One must first hear the sound and see the form before understanding arises.
Although one understands the teaching upon seeing a form, this relies on sound;
whereas understanding arises from smelling a fragrance without depending on sound.
Therefore, it is accepted that names and so forth depend on fragrances and so forth; thus, the former interpretation is superior.
These names, phrases, and so forth are established based upon visible form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects];
thus, there is no scriptural prohibition against this, nor does it contradict reason. Question: Since sound is produced by internal effort, could names and so forth be identical to that sound?
If fragrance arises only when external conditions are present, then names and so forth should not exist [independently]. Answer: Internal fragrance also arises through effort;
just as sound acquires a name.
External fragrance is like water and forests;
what contradiction to reason is there in its name?
For understanding arises from smelling the fragrance and so forth. If that is so, then awakening also arises based on the signified object.
Question: Should names and so forth also be established based on those [objects]? Answer:

Because one understands the signifier only through the signified, names, phrases, and so forth do not depend upon the signified. Question: The Sūtra says that the Buddha’s work is performed by means of fragrance.
Thus, based on fragrances and so forth, words, names, and phrases are established.
The Sūtra also states: "There are some buddha-fields that are silent and wordless;
in others, the work of a Buddha is performed through empty space alone."
Is it that names and phrases are established based on those very [factors] such as non-verbal expression?
Answer: What fault is there in establishing names?
It is just like the case where [names and phrases] are established based on volition (*cetanā*) and so forth; that is precisely how it is.
The statement that names are "without reliance on sound" means they are "wordless.
This does not contradict reason. Question: Since names and so forth are not established in reliance upon sound, there should be neither sound nor the ear.
Answer: In this land, the teachings are not established in reliance upon fragrance and so forth.
Since odors and so forth are not non-existent, those sounds and the ear likewise exist.
Commentary.
Regarding the phrase "arising from many dharmas of body and speech" and so forth:
for now, the term "many" is distinguished based on what is produced;
however, logically, it may also be called "many" in reference to the factors being prevented.
Commentary:
Regarding "the life-faculty and so forth," there are six things that are sustained.
That which can maintain its existence throughout its lifespan is given many names;
this is the correct response to the aforementioned external objection.
Non-informative matter (avijñapti) depends upon many [factors].

The physical basis—the matter of body and speech—is subsumed under the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and sound (*śabdāyatana*); however, because it supports the non-informative (*avijñapti*), it is subsumed under the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is likewise; its categories are similar to those of "name" (*nāman*) and so forth.
Length and so forth are not so; therefore, they are the same as the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
[Commentary].
There is an interpretation that [it] is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
If that is so, then why does this external statement single out and criticize me? To examine this in detail:
Based on the actual facts and established according to volition,
the non-informative (avijñapti) is indeed a single dharma;
this explanation is without contradiction.
If one points out this difficulty and explains the non-informative (avijñapti) based on what has been produced,
the former interpretation is superior.
[Commentary:]
Regarding the phrase "the other ten kinds of dharmas" and so forth:
there are twenty-four [dharmas] that are not associated with the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the explanation of the fourteen.
The remaining ten types should be understood by analogy with the above;
therefore, they are not mentioned here. Thus says the treatise.
Regarding those who maintain that the *anuśayas* (latent dispositions) and so forth [are substantial entities], according to the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*,
the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools state:
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) are neither mind nor mental factors (caitta),
nor do they have an object of cognition (ālambana).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are distinct from the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and are dissociated from the mind. Question: What is the intended meaning? Answer: The intended meaning is that the latent dispositions are themselves [the afflictions of] greed and so forth.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also of ten kinds.
Even when one is in a state without mind (*acittaka*) or when giving rise to wholesome states,
one is designated as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth due to the presence of these latent dispositions.

If these were mental factors (caitta), then since they would be absent during states such as the mindless ones (acittaka), there would be no defilements present; consequently, those states should be designated as belonging to an Arya.
If, on the other hand, they do exist in those states...
What are called "mindless," "virtuous mind," and so forth?
It is on account of these that they are reckoned as being dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
[Commentary:]
This meaning is that it is most coarse in its mental nature;
this is why the Sarvāstivāda school is called "coarse.
If the *paryavasthāna* (envelopments) are manifest activities (*samudācāra*).
The meanings of manifest entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) and latent disposition (*anuśaya*) are not compatible.
That which is called a "latent disposition" follows sentient beings, lying dormant and not arising.
If it were a manifest entanglement, it would not be continuous.
Because they are not latent in the sense of being dormant, the name "anuśaya" (proclivity) and its meaning are both inconsistent [with that definition]. Question:
How is it known that the Sarvāstivāda school considers *anuśayas* to be manifest? Answer: According to the nineteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:
The Vaibhāṣika masters state as follows:
"The essence of sensual desire and so forth is itself the latent disposition (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, they say:
"The Abhidharma speaks in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
Thus, the various afflictions are designated as "latent tendencies" (anuśaya).
Therefore, the Treatise states that the latent tendency of sensual desire is associated with three roots.
Since it is said to be "associated," [it must be so].
It is clearly evident. Regarding this, there is an interpretation that poses a question:
Since the Mahāyāna takes defiled seeds as the nature of the *anuśaya* (latent dispositions), an external critic might also object as follows:
According to your school, the seeds of the afflictions should not be called "latent dispositions" (anuśaya),
because they are designated as "greed" and so forth,
just like manifest greed and the like.
Answer: In our school, latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can only be described as the seeds of greed and so forth;
they are not themselves called "greed" and so on.
Therefore, your reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
If that is so, this principle is not without application to me;
however, it can only be described as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and so forth,
but cannot be called greed itself.
The reason established by the proponent of the treatise is likewise unestablished.
One should reflect upon this objection. To explain in detail:
it is designated as the cause of greed and so forth.
The destruction of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is not non-associated [with the mind],
yet they are included among the latent dispositions because they do not obstruct it;
why, then, does this reason not likewise refute the claim that the seeds of defilement are not called latent dispositions?
This greatly deviates from the intent of the treatise.
If it is argued that the Mahāsāṃghikas and others raised this objection,
one should not then say that in our own school, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are not designated as greed and so forth.
Why is this so? Just as the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu) are designated as "eighteen elements" according to their manifest names,
why is it that the latent tendencies (anuśaya), such as craving, are not likewise [designated] in the same way?
Furthermore, if latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) were not designated as "greed" and so forth, then these latent dispositions would not be greed and so forth.
If you grant this, then under which category of phenomena (*dharma*) would these latent dispositions be subsumed?
Therefore, [that position] is untenable.
Now, we establish a counter-argument against that reason: in our own school, the defiled seeds are definitively the *anuśayas*, which are designated as "greed" (*rāga*) and so forth.
Because there is no object of perception (*ālambana*),
just as you have no fault when addressing the great assembly regarding latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
If the opponent should offer this defense:
If one says, "I am also like that," one should challenge them as follows:
"While you do not admit that it is included among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*), you nonetheless allow that it does not obstruct the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, one should directly reprimand them, saying:
In our school, the defiled seeds are designated as "greed" and so forth;
they are subsumed under the mental factors (caitta) that manifest as greed and so on.
In your school, how are the latent tendencies (anuśaya) designated as greed and so forth subsumed within the category of non-associated [formations] (viprayukta)?
Treatise: Regarding those who maintain that there exists something else, distinct [from the mind], and so forth;
according to the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
The Saṃmitīya school states that non-informative [action] (avijñapti) and the afflictions (kleśa) are dissociated (viprayukta).
Some say this dharma is called "non-destruction" (avipraṇāśa);
by virtue of this dharma, one is able to obtain future desirable and undesirable fruits.
The same applies to mental karma.
It is accepted that this dharma exists;
for if it were not so, it would be severed and extinguished whenever another state of mind arises.
If such a distinct dharma were not produced within the continuum of the mind,
how could one obtain the fruit of a future life? Therefore,
one must certainly admit that this dharma exists.
This dharma truly exists;
it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
The remainder is as clarified in the commentary.
Treatise:

Regarding the first point, "dharmas known through direct perception," there is one interpretation which holds that it does not mean that form (*rūpa*) and so forth are called "known through direct perception" simply because they are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it is claimed that the mind and so forth are the objects of the knowledge of others' minds,
how can it be said later that they are "commonly known by the world"?
For the objects of the knowledge of others' minds are not commonly known by the world.
Furthermore, if [an object] were designated as "known through direct perception" (pratyakṣa) by virtue of another's mind,
then the eyes and so forth should also be included among those known through direct perception,
because the Buddha’s mind perceives the eyes and so forth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, it is known that what is commonly understood by the world is called "presently known. To this, [the author] says in detail:
If what is commonly understood by the world is termed "presently known," why are three categories established?
How could it be that people of the world do not understand this?
For we currently see that the world uses terms such as "eye" and "ear.
If you say that they do not understand because they do not know the essential nature and characteristics of the eye and so forth, [then...]
How could the world understand the essential nature and characteristics of the mind and so forth?
Since jars and the like are known through direct perception,
why is it necessary to speak of them separately?
Therefore, one should know that when the treatise states "that which is known through direct perception," it speaks in reference to what may exist within the worldly realm,
and not with respect to everything.
Because the knowledge of others' minds exists as something attained within the world,
whereas the five sense-faculties are never attained as worldly phenomena in the present.
Although the eighth [consciousness] takes such objects, it is not mentioned here because its existence as a distinct entity is not universally established.
Because there are differences in meaning among these three categories, they are distinguished separately. Thus,
following the original commentary (*śāstra*), it says:
Regarding the phrase "because it is a nature manifested by form, mind, and so forth":
this refers to a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi) concerning the manifestation of the characteristics of form and mind.
The first is: manifesting form by means of form.
Second, revealing the mind by means of form;
both are as explained in the sub-commentary.
Third, revealing the mind by means of the mind.
This refers to the knowledge of others' minds.
Fourth, form is manifested by the mind;

that is, the mind takes form as its object. Question: How can unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) be form, and how can they be manifested by the mind? Answer: According to one interpretation, the unconditioned phenomenon of space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*) is both form and manifested by the mind.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because the five aggregates have no location, they manifest as space;
furthermore, because the mind takes space as its object, it is called 'manifesting as mind' (*cittābhāsa*)."
If the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is based on that which is manifested by the mind alone as its means of realization,
or if it is based on the severance of self-nature through liberation from bondage,
it too is manifested by the mind alone.
Because the abandonment of defilements is manifested through the mind of discernment,
it is generally stated that the three types of abandonment are both form and mental manifestation;
this is because they are realized by means of abandoning the five aggregates.
Alternatively, it may be manifested by mind alone;
however, if it is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is manifested by both matter and mind,
because it is manifested through the opening of the conditions for matter and mind.
The immovable [state] is manifested by mind alone, as are perception and feeling;
its meaning is thus understandable.
Now, this [passage] generally clarifies the causes of all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
In general, it is said that their nature is manifested by form, mind, and so forth. [The opponent] asks:
"If you use such reasons to refute them, then the other party may likewise use these same reasons to refute the Mahāyāna."
Your *tathatā* and so forth are not devoid of the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) apart from consciousness,
because they are of the nature of that which is known (*jñeya*).

Just as with form, mind, and so forth, this measure should also be established as a valid refutation. [Objection: This incurs the fault of the thesis and its characteristics being mutually dependent. [Response:
In the Mahāyāna, the unconditioned is neither identical to nor separate from mind, form, and so forth.
Now, the objection is not a fault because it does not depart from [the original position]. If that were so, the opponent would be altering their thesis;
how then could one reconcile the claim that it is not the case that it is neither identical to nor separate from the nature of the unconditioned consciousness?
Answer: This too commits the fallacy of mutual dependence.
The path of mind and speech is quiescent and non-existent; it is beyond existence and non-existence, identity and difference, and so forth.
It negates fixed identity and difference, yet is itself neither identical nor different.
(Commentary)
Regarding the third case as a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound):
the third case is called the "instrumental" (*karaṇa*) and is also called the "agentive" (*kartṛ*).
Because it is manifested by the severance of delusions through the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), it belongs to the category of "by means of" (*yena*);
furthermore, there are other meanings,
as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
Commentary:

"That which is obtained through the power other than discernment is also like this" is likewise a third *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Question: Regarding the word "third" (*tṛtīya*), by what [reason] is it so called?
Now, one might ask: "By what means can they be considered the same if it is not through wisdom? The answer is:
although it is not through wisdom, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is manifested precisely because of the absence of conditions;
therefore, it is released in the third [moment].
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "that which is space is immovable," one interpretation holds that it is called "space" (ākāśa) because it cannot obstruct material objects.
It is called "empty" because it lacks form and so forth;
"voidness" (khu) is itself "emptiness" (k'ong).
This is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Detailed explanation follows:
That which is free from all obstructions is called space (*ākāśa*).
It cannot obstruct objects. Regarding the phrase "without color and so forth": it means that space lacks the characteristics of form and other such sensory qualities.
All [of these] have the meaning of being free from obstructions. Since their meanings are not distinct,
how can they constitute a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound)?
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that "space contains and receives phenomena such as form," if a phenomenon exists both internally and externally, it is called "pervasive" and "empty."
However, that which exists outside of phenomena cannot be called "pervasive" by virtue of being contained within them.

Since space can accommodate each phenomenon with which it comes into contact, the essence of space must not be unitary as it conforms to those various entities. Question: If space conforms to each phenomenon, then it would be difficult to establish that it is manifold.
Is this not to contradict one's own teaching?
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says:
"For example, although space pervades all various forms and diverse characteristics,"
Yet it cannot be said that there are various characteristics;
its essence is of a single flavor.
The Tathāgata’s dharma-realm is likewise so.
The meaning of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is also the same. Answer: The nature of emptiness (*ākāśa*) in the Mahāyāna is not a substantial entity.
That which lacks material obstruction is conventionally designated as "space.
Because it is devoid of phenomena and unobstructed, it pervades all forms.
Although it pervades all forms, it lacks intrinsic nature and remains unchanging;

since its essential substance is without differentiation, it is said to be of a single flavor. Question: The following clarifies that space is established in dependence upon suchness and consciousness.

How can it be said that its nature is non-existent? Answer: That sutra merely designates the locus devoid of substantial obstruction as "space. How is this verified? Answer: The sutra uses space as a metaphor for the pure *dharmadhātu*.
If one takes the space as it is established [in scripture] as the basis,
then there would be no distinction between the dharma of the simile and the dharma of the subject; therefore,
we take the transformation of consciousness as the basis.
The transformation of consciousness into conditioned phenomena cannot serve as an analogy;
therefore, that sutra says:
Just as various forms and appearances manifestly arise and manifestly perish within space,
yet this space itself has neither arising nor perishing; so too,

within the Tathāgata’s pure dharma-realm, the various manifestations of knowledge that transform and benefit sentient beings manifestly arise and manifestly perish, yet the pure dharma-realm has no arising or perishing.
Therefore, one should know that "not grasping" refers to the transformation of consciousness.
As for the treatise stating, "all dharmas should be mutually pervasive":
What is the intent of this objection? The answer is: that [opponent] maintains that space is one and yet conjoins with dharmas.
The previous objection was that space, by conforming to the entities it joins, should become manifold;
now the charge is that the entity which joins should, by conforming to the space it joins, become one.
If they were mutually pervasive, they could be called a single substance;
if they are not pervasive, how can they be called one? One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
That phenomenon should pervade this phenomenon,
because one clings to the essence of those two phenomena as being identical.
That should be understood in this way;
it is likewise the same as the twenty-fold refutation of the Vijñaptimātra [doctrine] regarding the lack of sequential activity and so forth.
(Commentary)
Regarding the statement that "transforming space into formless things and so forth that possess resistance":
this refers to the obstructive characteristics of phenomena such as the formless (*arūpa*).
[Commentary].

Regarding the statement that "the one contaminated consciousness is the cause, etc.," as clarified in the *Yideng* (The Lamp of Meaning): some say that the "one contaminated consciousness" refers exclusively to the sixth consciousness;
the "two uncontaminated consciousnesses" refer to the *miao guan* (sublime contemplation) and the *pingdeng* (equality) [consciousnesses].
Regarding the ultimate fruit, it is designated as the "cause.
As for the three types of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that constitute the fruit, these belong exclusively to the stage of Buddhahood;
therefore, they are called the "fruit. Detailed explanation follows:
Although this principle is also applicable,
since the Dharma Master was a disciple who had entered the inner chamber [of the teacher],
he followed the correct version based on the lamp.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that these manifested appearances are conventionally designated as "permanent" and so forth,
according to the eighteenth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚論), it says:
Regarding unconditioned space:
it is established as permanent because the objective aspect manifested by the mind resembles [space],
not because the mind takes that [space] as its object.

Because those objective spheres sometimes undergo transformation, it is asked: does the transformation of consciousness produce distinct seeds through perfuming? It is answered: solitary images arise from the seeing-part and do not produce distinct seeds through perfuming.
This is explained in detail in the *Dīpa*. One interpretation holds that there is distinct perfuming;

as the treatise itself states: "Due to the power of repeated practice, when the mind and its associates arise, they manifest the appearances of space and so forth, in accordance with conceptual discrimination."
Because unconditioned characteristics, such as those of space, appear,
we know that seeds are formed through distinct perfuming.
These characteristics produced by conditions are in reality conditioned phenomena.
The phenomena of arising and ceasing are similar from beginning to end;
because they appear to be one, permanent, and so forth, they are described as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and non-arising/non-ceasing.
Therefore, they are termed "provisional" (*prajñapti*). Detailed explanation: Although it is said that through repeated cultivation, the mind gives rise to an appearance resembling emptiness.
Yet it is stated that this does not refer to a distinct perfuming of seeds.
This is explained in detail in the *Dengpò* (Lamp Refutation). [End of] Commentary.
Regarding the nine unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) according to the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools:
the first three types are each a single entity in essence;
they manifest various states, yet their substance does not become manifold.
Next, the four [formless attainments], such as emptiness and so forth, are the bases for the four formless realms.
There exists a separate unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta) subsumed under cessation (nirodha);
one must first obtain this cessation and rely upon it before those [attainments] can arise.

The subtle five aggregates that serve as the basis are themselves impermanent, while the four formless [aggregates] that serve as their support are permanent. Question: Why is this not the case in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer: Because the aggregates there are not subtle, and that realm is not supremely excellent.
This is because the mind and its associated factors, which serve as the basis, can take objects of higher or lower levels as their cognitive objects without obstruction;
this is not the case for the formless realms (*ārūpya*), wherein the mind does not take lower levels as its objects.
Since there are obstructions and impediments,
there must be a separate unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) entity that serves as their basis.
The nature of the factors of dependent origination refers to the phenomena of birth and death.
It is certain that volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and the rest arise only after ignorance (*avidyā*),
and it is certain that ignorance and the rest exist prior to volitional formations and the rest;
this principle is one and the same.
The nature is eternally determinate.
Ignorance and the like are subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
their principle is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because there is a distinct principle governing this cycle of birth and death, it is capable of acting as an obstruction until its exhaustion;
therefore, ignorance arises first, followed by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all noble paths (*āryamārga*) is capable of bringing about detachment from defilements.
Principle is eternally one;
the eightfold distinctions are themselves subject to arising and ceasing.
Principle is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because there exists a distinct principle capable of obstructing [the end],
the path is determined by its sequential distinctions to be able to abandon suffering and so forth;
in reality, this is true for all noble paths.

In this context, the eightfold path is mentioned as a representative selection of the preeminent factors. Regarding the nine unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) according to the Mahīśāsaka school, the commentary states: [the list includes] space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the realm of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the realm of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the realm of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayita-nirodha*).
The three [attainments], such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), each have a single individual substance.
The "obstruction of meditative concentration" is termed *iñjita*, which refers to mental agitation (*vikṣepa*).
Because one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by severing this agitation, it is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
The three entities— wholesomeness and so forth— are each identical with True Suchness (tathatā),
and their nature is exclusively wholesome.
The factors of the path and dependent origination are the same as those of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement "among the three cessations, one establishes the cessation of impermanence and so forth," this means that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the cessation of impermanence (*anityatā-nirodha*) are termed the three cessations.
Regarding "cessation through impermanence":
this refers to the characteristic of cessation among the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
It is not only the two types known as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that are termed unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This very characteristic of cessation is also subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is because this unconditioned possesses functional power that it causes phenomena to pass away and cease.
Were it otherwise, both the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) would both be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
How can a characteristic cause that which is characterized to cease?
Therefore, we know that the characteristic of cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is as clarified in the *Vibhāṣā* (T. 1545), fascicle 38. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (T. 1509), fascicle 42:
There are three kinds of cessation:
cessation through knowledge of conditions (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through knowledge of conditions (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation through impermanence (*anityatā-nirodha*).
It is not said that cessation through impermanence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.
Regarding the commentary’s mention of "in terms of expression and in terms of principle," etc.:
"Designation" (abhilāpa) means "to designate and manifest.
Anything that can manifest a phenomenon is termed a designation;
it is not only names and so forth that alone are called designations.
The three natures are distinct;
because principle follows its verbal expression, they are divided into three types,
yet when discussing the principle itself, it is one.
It is simply named "True Suchness" (Tathatā).
[In the] Commentary:
"As for the lack of a separate explanation of the name..."
However, the term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) alone does not constitute the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vigraha*),
because there is no separate synthesis [of its members].
This is the case when one speaks of "unconditioned space" (*ākāśāsaṃskṛta*) and so forth.

All are *karmadhāraya* compounds, as explained in the previous commentary. According to one interpretation, the term "cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*) belongs to perception and feeling;
it is a *karmadhāraya* analysis.
The unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-asamskṛta) is an *tatpuruṣa* compound;
if "cessation" (*nirodha*) is unconditioned, it is the cessation of perception and feeling,
which is an *tatpuruṣa* compound.

The unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-asamskṛta*) is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, because one attains the unconditioned by relying on the immovable earth.
The unconditioned state of the immovable (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) is also a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. The detailed explanation states that the commentary follows the original text.
Since the principle is not contradicted,
the interpretation is also acceptable.
[End of] Commentary.
Regarding the statement that "all can be said to be provisional based on their provisional substance":
these eight kinds are established based on what is transformed by consciousness;
all eight kinds are provisional.
Commentary:
"The reality may also be so" means that if one relies on the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), all are real.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "by not obstructing a single dharma, one attains many unconditioned states," there are briefly three explanations. The first says: for instance, a single greed has nine distinct grades.
By severing this single craving, one realizes nine unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although the unconditioned has no categories, it is called "many" because it is spoken of in terms of what is severed. Second, this explains away external objections.
The meaning of the external objection is as follows:
Since one has already attained cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) by severing perception, feeling,
and so forth, for what reason is it further designated as the "unmoving unconditioned" (*āniñjya-asamskrta*) and so on?

Without obstructing the cessation of this single thought-moment, feeling, and so forth, one is able to realize the unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the immovable (*āniñjya*), and the many others. Third, it is said that by abandoning a single craving, one attains many unconditioned states.

The cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is established based on the abandonment of [defilements] such as those to be realized through direct experience; furthermore, one also attains many unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), such as the immovable (*āniñjya*).
The latter explanation is superior.
Commentary:
Regarding the absence of contradiction with one's own words:
the preceding statement that "the subject (dharmin) can apprehend that cognition" [is not contradicted].
The subsequent passage further states that it does not take that as its object.
Since it is said to be "capable of grasping," why does it not take that as its object?
And since it does not take that as its object, how can it be called "capable of grasping"?
Therefore, there is a contradiction. [Response:
Since the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) indicates that this is your own statement, there is no such fault.
Commentary.
There is no contradiction with our own tenet:
the subject of the thesis (dharmin) states that it can apprehend that color,
which is a color external to that mind.
In our own school's tenet, material phenomena external to the mind do not exist,
nor are they apprehended by the mind;
to now claim that one apprehends them contradicts our own tenet.
The Master’s position that your statement is likewise without fault is correct. Regarding the phrase in the Commentary,
"the faults of the two obstacles and the three stages":
The reading "tong" (penetration) in some editions is a scribal error.
"Guo" (transgression) refers to faults;
these faults of the two obstacles persist throughout the three stages (*vihāra*).
Commentary:
There are those who possess only the seeds of the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
such as the attachment to phenomena arising in an Arhat.
It is like a lamp possessing brightness. Regarding the commentary’s phrase,
"Furthermore, that which is equally transformed," etc.:
When it transforms appearing as a self, it necessarily transforms appearing as dharmas;
when it transforms appearing as dharmas, it does not necessarily possess a self.
The same applies to the statement [of the transformation].
This also includes the two aforementioned attachments.
Regarding the treatise’s statement, "taking as objects the aggregates, bases, and elements transformed by consciousness":

Question: Since it is said that [the objects] are "transformed," how many among the eight consciousnesses are "transforming consciousnesses" (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*)? The tradition offers three interpretations: First, it is said that this refers exclusively to the other seven consciousnesses, excluding the sixth.
The sixth [consciousness] that undergoes transformation is the direct object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana*).
This is because the subsequent text specifically states that it arises by grasping the manifestation of its own mind as a phenomenon. Second, it is said to be common to all eight [consciousnesses];
although the transformation of the sixth is indeed a direct object-condition.
The initial passage provides a general explanation.

There is no fault in the subsequent passage providing a specific explanation regarding the immediate object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), as it serves to clarify that this refers exclusively to the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness).
Therefore, it is stated that there is only an immediate object-condition.
Since they are the very basis for attachment, the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
They are identical to the aforementioned aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha), differing only in their classification and grouping. One interpretation states:
